name: Saladin
info: Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub (c. 1137 – 1193), known as Saladin, was a Sunni ruler of Kurdish origin who founded the Ayyubid dynasty, became the first sultan of Egypt and Syria, and took Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.

facts.born: c. 1137 in Tikrit, in present-day Iraq, to a family of Kurdish Rawadiya ancestry; son of Najm al-Din Ayyub, warden of the fortress of Tikrit
facts.died: 4 March 1193 (27 Safar 589 AH) at Damascus, of a fever; buried in a mausoleum in the garden outside the Umayyad Mosque
facts.role: Vizier of Fatimid Egypt from 26 March 1169; ruler of Egypt after the end of the Fatimid Caliphate in 1171; declared Sultan of Egypt and Syria by the Abbasid caliph in 1175; founder of the Ayyubid dynasty
facts.known: Founding the Ayyubid dynasty; abolishing the Fatimid Caliphate; uniting Egypt and Syria under one ruler; the victory at Hattin in 1187; the capture of Jerusalem; the war against Richard I in the Third Crusade; a reputation for generosity in Muslim and Christian sources

t: Saladin rose in the service of the Zengid ruler Nur al-Din, became vizier of Fatimid Egypt in 1169 and two years later ended the Fatimid Caliphate.
After Nur al-Din's death in 1174 he took Damascus and then most of Muslim Syria and Upper Mesopotamia, largely at the expense of his former master's family.
His victory at Hattin and capture of Jerusalem in 1187 provoked the Third Crusade, which ended in 1192 with Jerusalem still in his hands.
dyk: At his death Saladin had in his possession one piece of gold and forty pieces of silver; he had given away his wealth to his poor subjects and left nothing to pay for his funeral.
ev: Saladin is born in Tikrit, by his biographer's account on the night his family left the town
The Fatimid caliph al-Adid appoints him vizier of Egypt after the death of his uncle Shirkuh
Al-Adid dies and the Abbasid caliph is proclaimed in Cairo, ending the Fatimid Caliphate
After Nur al-Din's death he rides to Damascus with 700 horsemen and enters it amid general acclamation
He defeats the Zengids at the Horns of Hama and is declared Sultan of Egypt and Syria
He largely annihilates the Crusader army at Hattin and Jerusalem capitulates to him
The Treaty of Jaffa with Richard I ends the Third Crusade
He dies of a fever at Damascus

sections.early:
Saladin was born in Tikrit in present-day Iraq. His personal name was Yusuf; Salah ad-Din is an honorific meaning "Righteousness of the Faith". His parents were of Kurdish Rawadiya ancestry and had come from the village of Ajdanakan near Dvin in central Armenia. His father, Najm al-Din Ayyub, was warden of the fortress of Tikrit, where in 1132 he gave refuge to the defeated army of Imad al-Din Zengi, Atabeg of Mosul. In 1137 the family was banished from Tikrit after Ayyub's brother Asad al-Din Shirkuh killed a friend of the governor; according to Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad, Saladin's contemporary biographer, he was born the night they left.

In 1139 the family moved to Mosul, and Zengi made Ayyub commander of his fortress at Baalbek. Saladin later lived in Damascus; Zengi's son Nur al-Din became leader of the Zengids. Information on his childhood is scarce. Several sources claim that he was more interested in religious studies than in joining the military; he knew the genealogies and histories of the Arabs and the Hamasah of Abu Tammam by heart, spoke Kurdish and Arabic, and knew Turkish and Persian.

His military career began under his uncle Shirkuh, a commander of Nur al-Din. In 1164, aged 26, he accompanied Shirkuh's expedition to restore Shawar as vizier of the Fatimid caliph al-Adid in Egypt. At the Battle of al-Babein, west of Giza, he commanded the right wing of the Zengid army, though Muslim sources of the time place him with the baggage of the centre. In 1167 he was left to hold Alexandria and withstood a siege by a larger Crusader–Egyptian force for three months.
sections.rise:
In 1168 Amalric I of Jerusalem invaded Egypt and besieged Cairo, and Shawar again asked Nur al-Din for help. Shirkuh and Saladin arrived in 1169, Amalric withdrew, and Shirkuh had Shawar executed and became vizier, but died later that year. Al-Adid appointed Saladin in his place. The accounts differ on why: Ibn al-Athir claims the caliph was told that "there is no one weaker or younger" than Saladin, while Imad al-Din al-Isfahani wrote that the Zengid emirs forced the caliph to "invest him as vizier". He was inaugurated on 26 March.

Later that year he learned of a plot against him and had its chief conspirator, the controller of the Fatimid palace, arrested and killed. The next day 50,000 Black African soldiers of the Fatimid army revolted; by 23 August he had quelled the uprising. Towards the end of 1169 he defeated a Crusader–Byzantine force near Damietta. He gave members of his family high positions and founded colleges of Sunni law. In 1171, urged by Nur al-Din, he restored Abbasid suzerainty: al-Adid died on 13 September, and five days later the Abbasid caliph was named in the Friday sermon in Cairo.

His brother Turan-Shah drove off the Nubians and in 1174 was sent to conquer Yemen. In the early summer of 1174 Nur al-Din was mustering an army, apparently against Egypt, but he died on 15 May, leaving an eleven-year-old son, as-Salih. When the emir of Damascus asked for help against Aleppo, Saladin crossed the desert with 700 picked horsemen and entered Damascus on 23 November amid general acclamation.
sections.deeds:
From Damascus Saladin set about taking the cities that had belonged to Nur al-Din. He took Hama, besieged Aleppo, and captured the citadel of Homs in March 1175. On 13 April 1175 he defeated the combined Zengid forces of Mosul and Aleppo at the Horns of Hama. He then proclaimed himself king, dropped as-Salih's name from the Friday prayers and the coinage, and was declared "Sultan of Egypt and Syria" by the Abbasid caliph. A second victory at the Sultan's Mound in 1176 led to a treaty in which Aleppo recognised his sovereignty over his conquests.

Back in Cairo he had the city walls repaired and extended and began the Cairo Citadel. He left Egypt for the last time on 11 May 1182. In northern Mesopotamia he took Edessa, Raqqa and Nusaybin and captured Amid, but failed to take Mosul; Aleppo was handed to him by negotiation on 12 June 1183, and a peace was signed with Mosul in March 1186.

After Raynald of Châtillon attacked a Muslim caravan during a truce, Saladin resolved to topple the Kingdom of Jerusalem. On 4 July 1187 at the Battle of Hattin the Crusader force was largely annihilated and Guy of Lusignan, king consort of Jerusalem, captured. Saladin took almost every Crusader city, and Jerusalem capitulated on 2 October 1187 after a siege. Under the terms, each Frank could buy freedom for a ransom; Saladin let many families who could not pay leave, about 18,000 of the poor were ransomed by a collection, and another 15,000 were left to be enslaved. He permitted Jews to resettle in the city.
sections.opponents:
Saladin's first opponents were Muslim. His Zengid rivals in Syria claimed that he had "forgotten his own condition" as a servant of Nur al-Din and risen "in rebellion against his Lord" by besieging his master's son. The Order of Assassins, at odds with him since he replaced the Fatimids, twice tried to kill him, in May 1175 and at the siege of A'zaz in 1176; he laid waste their countryside in August 1176 without taking a fort, and later maintained cooperative relations with their leader Sinan. Among Egyptian Shi'as he is called "Kharab al-Din", "the destroyer of religion", for dismantling the Fatimids.

He suffered defeats. On 25 November 1177 Baldwin IV of Jerusalem surprised his army at Montgisard, and he fled to Egypt on a camel with a small remnant. He twice besieged Raynald's fortress of Kerak without success, and Tyre, under Conrad of Montferrat, withstood two sieges.

His wars had their cruelties. In 1178 he had Crusader captives executed for "plundering and laying waste the lands of the Faithful"; in 1183 the 170 survivors of Raynald's Red Sea raid were killed on his orders in various Muslim cities; and at Hattin he was personally responsible for the execution of Raynald. At Sinjar his soldiers broke discipline and plundered the city. At Jerusalem most of the foot soldiers were sold into slavery. According to Ibn Shaddad he "hated the philosophers"; in 1191 he ordered his son to execute the Sufi philosopher Yahya al-Suhrawardi in Aleppo. In Aleppo he replaced the Hanafi courts with Shafi'i administration despite a promise not to interfere.
sections.last:
Hattin and the fall of Jerusalem prompted the Third Crusade (1189–1192). King Richard I of England led the siege of Acre, took the city and executed almost 3,000 Muslim prisoners of war; Baha al-Din recorded differing explanations of the massacre and concluded, "God alone knows what the real reason was." On 7 September 1191 Saladin's forces suffered heavy losses at the Battle of Arsuf and were forced to withdraw. Richard occupied Jaffa, and Saladin dismantled the fortifications of Ascalon to keep the city from Crusader hands.

The two rulers exchanged envoys. Richard proposed that his sister Joan marry Saladin's brother, with Jerusalem as their wedding gift, but Saladin rejected the idea when Richard insisted that the brother convert to Christianity. In January 1192 Richard's army reached Beit Nuba, twelve miles from Jerusalem, and withdrew without attacking. In July Saladin besieged Jaffa and very nearly captured it before Richard arrived and defeated him outside the city. In the Treaty of Jaffa Richard agreed to demolish the fortifications of Ascalon and Saladin recognised Crusader control of the coast from Tyre to Jaffa; Christians could travel to Jerusalem as unarmed pilgrims, and there was to be peace for three years.

Saladin died of a fever at Damascus on 4 March 1193, not long after Richard's departure, and was buried in a mausoleum in the garden outside the Umayyad Mosque. Imad al-Din writes that he was survived by seventeen sons and one daughter; among them were al-Afdal, emir of Damascus, al-Aziz, sultan of Egypt, and al-Zahir, emir of Aleppo.
sections.legacy:
The Ayyubid dynasty that Saladin founded outlived him by only 57 years, and the Kingdom of Jerusalem persisted until the late 13th century, but 1187 marked a turning point in the Christian military effort in the region. In medieval Europe he was renowned as a model of kingship and of regal generosity. As early as 1202/03 Walther von der Vogelweide urged the German king to be more like him; Dante placed him among the virtuous non-Christians in limbo, and Boccaccio depicted him favourably. Lessing's play Nathan the Wise (1779) and above all Sir Walter Scott's novel The Talisman (1825) shaped the romantic modern view.

In the Muslim world his reputation had been largely forgotten, eclipsed by more successful figures such as Baybars of Egypt. The visit of the German emperor Wilhelm II to his tomb in 1898, coupled with anti-imperialist sentiment, encouraged the image of Saladin in the Arab world as a hero of the struggle against the West, building on the one created by Scott and other Europeans. With the rise of Arab nationalism in the 20th century his recapture of Palestine became an inspiration for opposition to Zionism, and the Eagle of Saladin became the symbol of revolutionary Egypt and of several other Arab states.

He has been described as the most famous Kurd in history and is a prominent figure in Arab, Turkish and Kurdish culture. Mark Cartwright writes that appreciation of his diplomacy and leadership in both Muslim and Christian sources of his time suggests that he "is indeed worthy of his position as one of the great medieval leaders".

summary: A Kurdish officer in Zengid service, Saladin became vizier of Egypt in 1169, ended the Fatimid Caliphate and united Egypt and Syria under his rule. He destroyed the Crusader army at Hattin and took Jerusalem in 1187, then held it against the Third Crusade until the Treaty of Jaffa of 1192.
references: Stanley Lane-Poole, Saladin and the Fall of the Kingdom of Jerusalem (G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1906)
Malcolm Cameron Lyons, Saladin: The Politics of the Holy War (Cambridge University Press, 1982)
Ben Duval, Saladin the Strategist: How the Crusaders Lost the Holy Land (Byzantine Emporia, LLC, 2022)
H.A.R. Gibb, The Life of Saladin: From the Works of Imad ad-Din and Baha ad-Din (Clarendon Press, 1973)
notes: The article's References and Bibliography are empty in the saved file; the references come from its Further reading and External links (Lane-Poole).

Birth: the lead gives c. 1137; the body says the family was banished from Tikrit in 1137 and that, by Ibn Shaddad, he was born that night. The article also says he was 26 in 1164, which would give 1138; I kept c. 1137.

Aleppo: the lead says 'By 1182, Saladin had completed the conquest of Syria after capturing Aleppo'; the body's sequence (Sinjar falls 30 December 1182, Harran February 1183, Tell Khalid 17 May, Aleppo 'On 12 June') puts it in 1183. I wrote 12 June 1183 and kept Aleppo out of the key events.
The article says the Abbasid caliph declared him Sultan of Egypt and Syria after the Horns of Hama (1175); the lead names the caliph al-Mustadi. No day is given.
The article's sentence that Saladin 'captured Gaza in 1187' and destroyed its fortifications in 1191, placed in a paragraph about 1170, is confused; left out, with the capture of Eilat.
Nubians: the article says they were driven off in summer 1173 and 'returned in 1173' again; I wrote only that Turan-Shah drove them off.
Hattin: the article gives no numbers for either army or the dead ('largely annihilated'); none given.

The 170 Red Sea raiders: the article dates al-Adil's letter 2 March (1183 by its sequence) and gives no date for the killings; I wrote 'in 1183', which is an inference from the sequence. The editor may prefer to drop the year.
Jerusalem ransom: the article gives no sum per head ('an unusually low ransom'); the figures 18,000 ransomed and 15,000 left to be enslaved are the article's.
The article does not name the brother proposed for Joan in the text (al-Adil is not named there); left unnamed.
Succession: the article does not describe how the realm was divided at his death; I gave only the sons' titles from Imad al-Din's list.
The cause of the 'attack on a Muslim caravan by Raynald' has no date in the article.
References: books about the person from the article's own bibliography sections (scripts/kinds/article-refs.js), chosen by title, in place of the draft's.
